summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law, while criminal law and official document rules remain Danish.

Same-sex relations are lawful, and the territory's record on partnership and marriage has been permissive for three decades. Partnership law was adopted from the Danish model in 1996 and passed with virtually no debate, and it has since been replaced by the marriage law.

Same-sex marriage came into effect on 1 April 2016. Greenland adopted Danish legislation that had passed unanimously twice in Denmark, the first bill lapsing after Danish elections, and the local parliament enacted it without recorded opposition; it replaced the 1996 partnership law. The bishop of the established church supported it. Registered partnerships had run from 1 July 1996 until the marriage law took effect, at which point the partnership law's application was repealed.

Transgender Greenlanders may change the sex designation on official identity documents. A law passed in 2016 by decree allows legal sex changes based on self-determination, with no requirement for sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or a medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want to change their documentation, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor in addition to male and female.

Since 2010 Greenland has outlawed hate speech: Article 100 of the Criminal Code prohibits speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories, alongside penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation.

Greenland's parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, taking effect on 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of "sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, [and] gender characteristics" among other characteristics. The law creates an Equal Treatment Board to manage discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights.

Public expression is visible: the first pride parade was held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010, attended by about 1,000 people, and a modest Pride march has run annually since 2010. Gay life is described as low-key, integrated and non-violent. There is virtually no gay scene due to the small, scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.

The national association LGBT Qaamaneq was founded in August 2014 for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, working for political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.
tangentialFactors:
The territory's small and scattered population concentrates social life in Nuuk, where the handful of nightclubs and bars draw a mixed gay and straight crowd; there is no distinct gay scene elsewhere. Visitors should expect visibility to be low rather than hostile.

Greenland's legal framework on partnership, marriage, hate speech and anti-discrimination tracks Danish national legislation, so developments in Denmark's parliament have historically been adopted locally with little or no recorded opposition. The 2016 marriage law and the 2016 document-change decree both followed this pattern.

The 2024 Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination is broader than sexual orientation alone, covering gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics, and it establishes an Equal Treatment Board and an Equality Council. This places complaint-handling machinery in the territory rather than relying solely on Danish institutions.

Discrimination complaints on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics are handled by the Equal Treatment Board established under the Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination, in force from 1 July 2024. outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state whether the 2024 anti-discrimination law's protections have been tested in any reported complaint before the Equal Treatment Board, nor any outcomes of such proceedings.

No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening practices specific to transgender travellers, including whether passport sex markers are checked against other documents.

The inventory does not resolve whether Article 100 of the Criminal Code explicitly lists gender identity among its protected categories, or whether hate-crime penalty enhancements have been applied in any case involving a transgender person.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare in Greenland, and any referral pathway to Danish services, is not sourced here.
